The topic: Right to Erasure
Additional context/details: Withdraw consent to data processing and ask for deletion.
Source/Reference: Bangladesh PDPO 2025
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Under Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025, withdrawal of consent and erasure are governed principally by Section 13, rather than Section 23. This is a historical account of the ordinance: the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 subsequently repealed it. The provisions described here should not be assumed to establish the law currently in force. A data-fiduciary is the person or organization responsible for processing personal data. Section 13 allows the data subject to withdraw consent wholly or partly for storage, processing, or automated decisions. Withdrawal does not retrospectively invalidate processing undertaken while consent remained effective. Under Section 10, rights are exercised through a written application to the data-fiduciary. The organization must consider the sensitivity of the data and the risk of fraud, retain an audit record of its actions, and inform the applicant. Section 13 identifies grounds for erasure, including the original purpose no longer existing, withdrawal of the consent on which processing depended, an objection made under the ordinance, unlawful processing, or deletion needed to meet a legal obligation or prescribed condition. The right is qualified. Section 13 also lists possible grounds for refusing deletion: identification-related data while consent continues, preservation or archival purposes, legal retention duties, and data classified as confidential or restricted. These are statutory categories, not permission to refuse every request. Section 14 provides for system-wide propagation of approved changes. The primary data-fiduciary verifies the deletion or update and notifies the National Data Management Authority. The Authority directs relevant secondary data-fiduciaries and processors to implement the approved change and records the changes and acknowledgments in an immutable ledger, using blockchain or equivalent technology. The process extends to copies in mirrors, caches, backups, disaster-recovery systems, test environments, and migration datasets. Regulations determine implementation timelines. Where erasure would distort a record, Section 14 permits refusal only for Authority-designated public-interest data or archival, scientific, or historical records. The refusal must give reasons and can be appealed. Section 43 prescribes an offence for continued storage, use, or disclosure after consent withdrawal or expiry of lawful retention, or failure to implement the required erasure, correction, or restriction without undue delay within 30 days of a request. Its maximum penalty is three years' imprisonment, BDT 500,000, or both. However, Section 1(3) deferred commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The prescribed penalty therefore must not be presented as automatically enforceable from the ordinance's publication date. For an erasure request, identify the relevant records, specify any consent being withdrawn, and ask for a written explanation of any retention ground or refusal.

The topic: Right to Erasure

Source/Reference: Bangladesh PDPO 2025
Persona: I have mid literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (Mid Literacy)

Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 gave people rights over their personal data. Section 13 covered taking back consent and asking for deletion. Consent means permission to use your data. The Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later replaced this ordinance. This explains the older rules, not the law now in force. The person or group in charge of using your data is the data-fiduciary. You could take back all or part of your consent. This could cover storage, other uses, or decisions made by a computer. Taking back consent did not make earlier lawful uses illegal. Under Section 10, you had to apply in writing. The group had to check the risk of fraud and how private the data was. It also had to keep a record of its actions and tell you what it did. Section 13 set out reasons for deletion. The data's first purpose might no longer exist. You might take back the consent used to process it. You might object under the ordinance. The group might have used the data against the law. A law or another rule might require deletion. Deletion was not always required. Section 13 also listed grounds for refusal. These included ID-related data while consent still applied. They also included records kept for preservation or archives. A law could require some records to be kept. Data classed as confidential or restricted was also listed. These grounds did not allow a group to reject every request. Section 14 dealt with changes across linked systems. The main group had to check that it had deleted or changed the data. It then had to tell the National Data Management Authority. This was the public body in charge. That body could direct other groups and data processors to make the same change. A processor uses data for the main group. A fixed record of changes and replies had to be kept. It could use blockchain or a similar system that cannot be altered. Changes also covered copies in mirrors, caches, and backups. They covered disaster-recovery systems, test systems, and migration datasets too. Rules set the time for these steps. A group could sometimes refuse deletion if it would distort a record. Section 14 limited this to certain records approved by the Authority. These were public-interest data or archival, scientific, or historical records. The group had to give reasons. You could appeal that refusal. Section 43 dealt with keeping, using, or sharing data after consent was withdrawn or lawful retention ended. It also covered failure to act on required deletion, correction, or restriction within 30 days without undue delay. It set a maximum of three years in prison, BDT 500,000, or both. But Section 1(3) delayed the start of Sections 31-46. They needed a government notice after 18 months from issue. Those penalties did not all start when the ordinance was issued. In your request, name the data you want deleted. Say which consent you are taking back. Ask for written reasons if the group keeps the data.

The topic: Children's Data Protection
Additional context/details: Requires parental consent and prohibits tracking for ads.
Source/Reference: Bangladesh Data Protection Ordinance 2025
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 provided child-specific safeguards in Section 9. This account concerns the ordinance, which was later repealed by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026; it should not be treated as a statement of current law. Section 2 defined a child as a person under 18 or an age specified by the government. Under Section 9, a data-fiduciary could collect or process a child's personal data through the prescribed procedure with consent from a parent, legal guardian, or person empowered to decide on the child's behalf. A data-fiduciary is the person or organization responsible for processing the data. Processing had to protect the child's rights and interests, rather than undermine them. Section 38 required prior verifiable parental or legal-guardian consent and reasonable steps to establish the consenting guardian's identity and authority. Consent therefore involved more than an unchecked assertion that someone was a parent. Section 9 prohibited using a particular child's behavior or other data for tracking, monitoring, profiling, or targeted advertising. Profiling means evaluating personal information to infer characteristics such as interests, habits, or behavior. This prohibition was distinct from the consent requirement: obtaining a parent's consent did not remove the child-specific restriction. The provision should not be restated as a ban on every advertisement or every processing activity involving a child. Section 9 also stated that the relevant consent remained valid until the child reached 18. For a person unable to consent, the corresponding consent lasted until that person gained the ability to consent. Section 38 prescribed a maximum of three years' imprisonment, BDT 500,000, or both for collecting, processing, or using a child's data without the required prior verifiable consent, or failing to take reasonable steps to verify the guardian's identity and authority. Section 1(3), however, delayed commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The existence of a prescribed penalty must therefore be distinguished from its immediate enforceability. The central distinction is between collecting data through a lawful consent process and using a child's behavior or data for prohibited tracking or advertising. Organizations had to address both duties; parental consent alone did not satisfy them all.

Consent had to come from a parent, legal guardian, or someone with power to decide for the child. Consent means permission. The child's rights and interests had to be protected, not harmed. Section 38 required prior consent that could be checked. The group also had to take reasonable steps to check the guardian's identity and right to give consent. A claim that someone was a parent was not enough on its own. Section 9 also banned using a particular child's behavior or other data for tracking, monitoring, profiling, or targeted ads. Section 38 set penalties for two kinds of breach. One was collecting, using, or processing a child's data without the required prior consent. The other was failing to take reasonable steps to check the guardian's identity and authority. The maximum was three years in prison, BDT 500,000, or both. These were maximum penalties, not fixed penalties for every case. Section 1(3) delayed the start of Sections 31-46. They needed a government notice after 18 months from issue. The topic: Unauthorized Data Collection
Additional context/details: Criminal penalties for disclosing data without authority.
Source/Reference: Bangladesh Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Unauthorized collection and disclosure were addressed by several distinct offences in Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025. This is an account of that ordinance, not current law: the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later repealed it. Personal data includes information that identifies a person or makes them identifiable, including financial, location, and biometric information. Processing is broader than collection: it includes storage, use, transfer, and disclosure. Absence of consent does not alone establish that every use is unlawful, because a relevant legal basis may also authorize processing. Section 36 addressed processing personal data, supplying, transferring, or disclosing it to a third party, or receiving it from a third party without the required consent or legal basis, with dishonest intent or an intention to benefit. Its maximum penalty was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. The intent requirement matters; this provision should not be described as imposing the same penalty on every accidental mistake. Section 37 addressed processing sensitive personal data in breach of Section 7 or another provision without explicit consent or another legal basis. Its maximum was seven years' imprisonment, BDT 2,000,000, or both. Sensitive data includes health information, religious beliefs, and biometric information. Section 39 covered unauthorized interception or extraction of personal data after gaining access to a system, device, or database, and interception of communications or data flows while personal data was being transmitted. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. Section 40 addressed obtaining consent by deception, force, impersonation, misrepresentation, or other unfair means; collecting or processing data on that basis; and knowingly receiving that data for a profitable or unfair purpose. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. Section 41 addressed disclosure, transfer, or use of sensitive or personally identifiable data obtained during official or contractual duties, and use or processing for a purpose not authorized under the ordinance. It covered data-fiduciaries, processors, employees, contractors, and agents. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,500,000, or both. Section 44 provided the same penalty as the underlying offence for a person or institution supporting, authorizing, or assisting its commission. Section 45 assigned trials of offences under the ordinance to the Cyber Tribunal. The ordinance did not prescribe a death penalty for these offences. Sections 54 and 55 concerned emergency orders and publication of an authoritative English text, not the prison and fine provisions. Section 1(3) deferred commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The listed penalties are prescribed maxima, not automatic sentences or proof that those provisions were enforceable immediately on publication. Compliance therefore required a valid consent or legal basis, genuine consent where required, access limited to authorized uses, and care when receiving or sharing another person's data.

The topic: Data License
Additional context/details: Users grant worldwide license to use their content.
Source/Reference: Facebook (Meta) ToS
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

A content licence permits Facebook to use material without transferring the user's intellectual-property ownership. The Facebook terms describe a non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, worldwide licence for protected content uploaded or shared in connection with its products, consistent with privacy and application settings. Non-exclusive means the owner can use the material and permit others to use it. Transferable and sub-licensable describe permissions Meta can pass or grant onward; they do not mean the user is assigning copyright. Royalty-free means this contractual permission does not require a royalty payment. Worldwide describes its geographic scope. The licence supports activities such as hosting, copying, distributing, displaying, translating, modifying, and creating derivative works. It should not be expanded into an unlimited right over all personal data: copyright permission, privacy rights, and lawful processing obligations are distinct. Nor should it be described as necessarily perpetual and irrevocable. The terms link the licence's end to deletion from Meta's systems, with qualifications for the deletion process, certain retention obligations, and material other people have shared or used under the licence. Account deletion is therefore not proof that every copy disappears immediately. Privacy settings matter to permitted sharing but do not prevent every independent recipient from keeping a copy. Before posting, consider the audience, whether you have rights to the material, and whether you are comfortable granting the stated uses. The applicable version of Facebook's terms governs; do not infer a permanent, unconditional grant from the word worldwide alone.

Your sharing settings matter, but another person may still keep a copy they received. Before posting, check who can see the content. Check that you have the rights to share it. The topic: Biometric Tracking
Additional context/details: Collection of faceprints and voiceprints from content.
Source/Reference: TikTok Privacy Policy (US)
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

The U.S. TikTok privacy-policy clause referenced in this topic states that TikTok may collect biometric identifiers and biometric information, including faceprints and voiceprints, from user content. Where applicable law requires permission, the clause says the required permission will be sought before collection. This is a qualified collection statement, not proof that every uploaded video generates an identity template or that a particular identification algorithm is deployed. Biometric information concerns measurable human characteristics. A faceprint can represent facial features numerically; a voiceprint can represent characteristics of a speaker's voice. These differ from recognizing an object in a video or transcribing spoken words. The policy also describes analysis of image and audio content, including objects, scenery, facial or bodily features, audio characteristics, and spoken text. Such analysis does not invariably constitute identity recognition. The clause should not be treated as a technical specification of geometric measurements, cryptographic signatures, moderation systems, or cross-platform identification. Likewise, an unspecified retention period must not be converted into a precise storage guarantee. Permissions and privacy rights depend on the applicable U.S. law and policy version; the clause does not erase statutory protections. Before uploading identifiable faces or voices, consider whose information the content contains, review the relevant privacy and permission notices, and use the available privacy-request channels. A face or voice may remain recognizable even when a username changes. The important distinction is between what the policy permits, what the service actually does in a particular situation, and what the law requires.

Persona: I have mid literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (Mid Literacy)

TikTok's U.S. privacy-policy clause says it may collect biometric information from content users provide. The examples named are faceprints and voiceprints. Biometric information is data about measurable features of a person. A faceprint can turn facial features into a numerical pattern. A voiceprint can describe features of a person's voice. These patterns are different from spotting a chair in a video or writing down the words someone says. The policy also describes looking at images and audio for objects, scenery, face and body features, sounds, and spoken text. That kind of analysis does not always identify a person.
